Predictive distribution of the event time

Source: R/predictEventTime.R
predictEventTime.Rd

Experimental. Each patient's whole predictive distribution of the event time \(T\) given the biomarker history and \(T > s\), \(p(t \mid Y, T > s) \propto f(Y \mid t) f(t)\) for \(t > s\), in one pass: the cumulative distribution function at prediction_time + horizons and its quantiles. The CDF at a horizon is predictRisk()'s risk (summed over the event types under competing risks), but computing the whole curve at once is much faster than calling predictRisk() once per horizon. The quantiles give prediction intervals for \(T\) itself, e.g. the 10\ time the patient outlives with probability 0.9.

Beyond the last follow-up of the survival sub-model the distribution rests on its extrapolated baseline hazard, so upper quantiles that fall there are only as good as that tail (see survivalSubExternal). Within follow-up the Breslow baseline puts the probability at the observed event times, so the CDF rises in steps there; quantiles are interpolated within the grid cell where the CDF crosses the probability.

Usage

predictEventTime(
  data_predict_all,
  long_fit_all,
  survival_fit_all,
  prediction_time,
  horizons,
  time_variable,
  survival_variable_all = NULL,
  survival_trans_function = NULL,
  probs = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9),
  n_grid = 200,
  n_tail = 100
)

Arguments

data_predict_all, long_fit_all, survival_fit_all, time_variable, survival_variable_all, survival_trans_function

As in predictRisk (right-censored survival fits only).

prediction_time

The landmark \(s\).

horizons

Times after prediction_time at which to evaluate the CDF.

probs

Probabilities of the quantiles.

n_grid

Grid cells between prediction_time and the last horizon or the survival sub-model's last follow-up, whichever is later; n_tail grid cells beyond it.

n_tail

See n_grid.

Value

An object of class "predictEventTime.BJM", a list with cdf (patients x horizons, \(P(T \le s + h \mid Y, T > s)\)); with competing risks, cif, a list of two such matrices, one per event type (0, 1; they sum to cdf); quantile (patients x probs, absolute times); prediction_time; horizons.

Examples

# \donttest{
data(pbc3)
surv <- survivalSub(pbc3[!duplicated(pbc3$id), ], Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex, NULL)
long <- longitudinalSub(pbc3[pbc3$status3 == 1, ], list(serBilir ~ year + age + years),
                        list(~ year | id))
history <- pbc3[pbc3$id %in% c(2, 7) & pbc3$year <= 3, ]
history$years <- NA
out <- predictEventTime(history, long, surv, prediction_time = 3, horizons = 1:5,
                        time_variable = "year")
out$cdf
#>           h1        h2        h3        h4        h5
#> 2 0.05116750 0.1195239 0.2082627 0.3702554 0.4548032
#> 7 0.03034362 0.0748631 0.1385939 0.2693125 0.3448145
out$quantile
#>        10%      50%      90%
#> 2 4.621278 8.441462 11.17829
#> 7 5.364772 8.990141 13.87635
# }
